PullRequest.Title: agentHost: add scoped permission rules and smart approvals
PullRequest.Body:
<!-- Thank you for submitting a Pull Request. Please:
* Read our Pull Request guidelines:
  https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/wiki/How-to-Contribute#pull-requests
* Associate an issue with the Pull Request.
* Ensure that the code is up-to-date with the `main` branch.

Replaces the tool-wide "Allow in this Session" approval for shell, URL, and file
tools in the agent host. The old approval allowed every later call of the tool. Now
the host offers scoped grants. The grants use permission rules in the format of
Claude Code. The local VS Code client keeps these rules in sync with its settings.

- Adds a permission rule parser and matcher for `Shell(...)`, `WebFetch(...)`,
  `Read(...)`, `Edit(...)`, and bare tool names. Shell rules support wildcard,
  `/regex/`, and `commandLine:` forms. WebFetch rules use VS Code URL patterns with
  https as the default scheme.
- Adds `permissions.ask` next to `allow` and `deny`. A deny rule rejects the call,
  also when Allow All is set. An ask rule always prompts. Rules from the chat, the
  session, and the host are combined.
- Changes the shell and URL confirmations. "Allow Once" is the default. The options
  are "Allow `cmd …` in this Session", "Allow Exact Command in this Session", "Always
  Allow …", "Allow Fetching <host> in this Session", and "Always Allow Fetching
  <host>". Read and write confirmations offer grants for the file and for the
  nearest git root folder. The option ID contains the grant rules, so a client
  cannot forge a grant.
- Moves the default terminal auto-approve rules to a shared platform module. VS Code
  and the agent host use the same rules. The host applies them only where no
  explicit rule matches.
- Syncs `chat.tools.urls.autoApprove`, `chat.tools.terminal.autoApprove`, and
  `chat.tools.terminal.ignoreDefaultAutoApproveRules` from user settings to the
  local agent host at start and when they change. "Always Allow" grants on the local
  host are written back to user settings. Remote agent hosts do not sync.
- Removes the client-generated terminal actions for agent host sessions and the
  `terminalAutoApproveRules` and `urlAutoApproveRules` root config keys.
- Adds an `AgentPermissionKind` const enum. Claude shell requests now use bash.
- Writes the host config to a temporary file and renames it. This prevents a host
  that starts at the same time from reading a partial file and losing values.

Fixes https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/341732

## Validation

Commands run on the merged branch:

- `npm run typecheck-client`: passed
- `npm run eslint -- <54 changed files>`: passed
- `npm run valid-layers-check`: passed
- `./scripts/test.sh --run <48 changed and affected test files>`: 4293 passing
- `./scripts/test.sh --run src/vs/platform/agentHost/test/node/copilotAgentSession.test.ts`: 1468 passing

Manual test plan: local agent host Copilot/Claude sessions with shell, URL, read, and write confirmations, local and remote host sync, and restart persistence. Test of the remote agent host flow and Windows paths was not done.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The added loop, concrete fs.promises.access implementation, awaited caller, and tests enumerating one probe per ancestor establish the mechanism and critical-path placement directly. Only the duration of each filesystem access and typical path depth are environment-dependent.
Findings.PerformanceResource: serial filesystem access calls for .git entries
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Each read/write confirmation performs one awaited filesystem access per ancestor between the target's parent and the first Git root, or all the way to the filesystem root when none exists; the work repeats for every prompted file because there is no cache or coalescing.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: increased confirmation latency and excessive filesystem I/O
Findings.PreviousBehavior: A pending read/write confirmation could be converted to ChatToolCallReady without probing ancestor directories for repository metadata.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The new path-option builder walks upward and awaits an existence check for .git at every directory before constructing and dispatching the confirmation action.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added RIGHT line 950 is the new awaited filesystem boundary inside the ancestor loop, and agentSideEffects.ts adds an await of this method before the UI-ready action is created.
Findings.Title: Cache or bound the Git-root lookup before showing file confirmations
Findings.Impact: For a file outside a repository, or in a deep checkout/network-mounted workspace, the confirmation card cannot appear until all ancestor filesystem requests complete. Repeated file prompts repeat the same walk, making agent interactions visibly stall and increasing I/O.
Findings.Evidence: _handleToolReady now awaits getPathConfirmationOptions at agentSideEffects.ts:1769 before createToolReadyAction and before dispatching the ready action. The added loop at lines 949-956 serially calls this._exists for each ancestor; the default is Promises.exists, implemented with fs.promises.access. Added tests explicitly expect /repo/src/.git, /repo/.git, and /.git probes when no repository is found, confirming depth-proportional cardinality.
Findings.Recommendation: Resolve the repository root from existing workspace/SCM metadata where possible, or memoize/coalesce ancestor results per directory and stop at a known workspace boundary; fall back to the direct parent without walking to the filesystem root.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The changed call path is explicit: _handleToolReady awaits getAutoApproval for every request; the added permission block calls _resolvePermissionRequests, and unmatched read/write requests then continue into the pre-existing _isReadAutoApproved or _isEditAutoApproved path, which calls _resolveResourcesForApproval again. Root permissions are populated with Shell/WebFetch approvals by this PR, so unrelated rules realistically activate the duplicate resolution. Exact filesystem latency varies by mount and path existence, which affects severity but not mechanism confidence.
Findings.PerformanceResource: filesystem realpath operations and ancestor probes for nonexistent paths
Findings.PerformanceScaling: For each read/write tool request, any nonempty allow or ask list adds one full realpath-resolution chain; unmatched requests then perform the existing chain again, and nonexistent targets can issue one realpath call per ancestor. A nonempty deny list adds another chain before this pass.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: increased tool approval latency and excessive filesystem I/O
Findings.PreviousBehavior: Per-tool permission checks were in-memory name lookups; read/write requests performed symlink resolution only in the existing read or edit auto-approval check.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: The added generic allow/ask block resolves every read/write path before checking whether any rule can target that permission kind, then the normal read/write auto-approval logic resolves the same path again when no rule matches.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: Added RIGHT line 286 introduces the first await of _resolvePermissionRequests in getAutoApproval; before this hunk, permission lookup did not touch the filesystem and only the later read/write validation resolved the path.
Findings.Title: Avoid resolving file paths twice for unrelated permission rules
Findings.Impact: After a user has any persistent shell or URL approval, each agent file read/write can incur duplicate realpath I/O before it proceeds. On deep, missing, network-mounted, or otherwise slow paths this delays auto-approval or the confirmation UI for every file operation in a turn.
Findings.Evidence: At the added line, getAutoApproval awaits _resolvePermissionRequests whenever any allow/ask rule exists. _resolvePermissionRequests calls _resolveResourcesForApproval for read/write paths (line 924). If an unrelated Shell/WebFetch rule or a nonmatching path rule does not approve, execution reaches _isReadAutoApproved (line 326) or _isEditAutoApproved (line 343), which call _resolveResourcesForApproval again at lines 648/782. resolveRealPathForNonexistent walks ancestors serially for missing targets. The same PR syncs terminal and URL approvals into root permissions, making unrelated nonempty rule lists a normal state.
Findings.Recommendation: Filter allow/ask rules by the request's tool/kind before resolving paths, and carry the resolved literal/real-path candidates through the remaining read/write auto-approval checks so each request resolves at most once.

Scenarios.Scenario: Agent-host read/write tool permission evaluation and confirmation rendering
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The pending-confirmation handler must complete deny evaluation and auto-approval before it can respond to the provider; if approval is still required, it also awaits path-option generation before dispatching ChatToolCallReady, so both realpath validation and the new Git-root lookup are on the user-visible critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Resolve the literal file path and symlink target, walking existing ancestors for a nonexistent target
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One added resolution chain whenever any allow/ask rule exists; unmatched requests then execute the pre-existing read/write resolution chain, and a deny list can add a third. Each missing-path chain can issue one realpath call per ancestor.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Permission-name lookup was in-memory and only the normal read/write auto-approval path performed realpath validation.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Probe each ancestor for a .git entry
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One serial fs access per ancestor until a Git root is found, or through the filesystem root; repeated independently for each prompted file.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: No repository-metadata filesystem probes occurred while constructing a file confirmation.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The ready action and confirmation card are not created until the walk finishes.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of file tool calls, path depth, number of missing ancestors, number of configured permission lists, and storage latency; effective cardinality is unchanged by grouping because paths are evaluated independently and there is no cache/coalescing.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Checks within one request are serial. Concurrent tool requests can launch independent realpath and Git-root walks without a shared limiter or coalescing.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No application cache exists for resolved request paths or nearest Git roots; only OS filesystem caches may make warm calls cheaper. Negative Git-root results are repeated.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: changed awaits, filesystem implementations, pre-existing second resolution, and test-asserted ancestor cardinality directly establish both mechanisms.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Local shallow paths may make each access cheap, while deep paths, missing targets, network mounts, and repeated agent edits make the delay substantially larger.
Scenarios.Verdict: Two reportable regressions: duplicate path resolution under unrelated rules and uncached serial Git-root discovery before rendering.

Scenarios.Scenario: Agent-host shell command approval and scoped-grant option generation
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Tree-sitter parsing and rule classification run synchronously in the host before auto-approval or confirmation dispatch. A deny list adds a separate deny parse, and an unresolved command is evaluated again to construct scoped options.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number and length of shell commands, parsed subcommands, and permission rules.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Each permission event evaluates independently on the event loop; there is no shared limiter, but parsing is synchronous and commands are normally short.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Tree-sitter grammars and compiled default rules are cached. Parse trees/evaluations are not cached per command.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for execution flow, lower for material user-visible magnitude.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Extra deny-pass parsing is real but command lines are typically small; this did not independently meet the threshold for another finding after accounting for the removed renderer-side parsing path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No additional finding; the PR also removes asynchronous renderer-side parsing, and the remaining added parse cost was not proven material independently.

Scenarios.Scenario: Approve-once, session grant, or host grant for shell and URL tools
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The confirmation response is dispatched to the host immediately. Mirroring a host-scoped grant into VS Code settings is fire-and-forget and therefore off the current tool's critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Update user configuration for URL and/or terminal approval settings
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Zero writes for session grants; one write per affected setting for a host grant, at most two for mixed URL/shell rules.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Agent-host confirmation did not mirror persistent grants into these user settings.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off the current approval critical path; writes are queued after confirmation dispatch.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of host-scoped user approvals, not number of ordinary tool calls.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: A module-level Sequencer serializes all mirror writes, preventing lost-update bursts; no unbounded parallel settings writes.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Each queued write re-inspects the latest user value, which preserves earlier writes; there is no negative cache, but grants are user-driven and low frequency.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Configuration persistence cost depends on the settings backend but is off path and low cardinality.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression because the expensive boundary is deliberately serialized and off the approval critical path.

Scenarios.Scenario: Local agent-host startup and permission-setting synchronization
Scenarios.CriticalPath: On host/root-state hydration or relevant user-setting changes, the contribution converts configured URL/terminal entries and dispatches structurally changed root config to the host. Startup waits for normal host hydration, but ordinary agent turns do not wait on subsequent mirror sync.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Dispatch root-config changes to the local agent host
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One dispatch per structurally changed forwarded key; permissions and ignore-defaults can produce two dispatches for a combined settings change.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Terminal rules were forwarded by the protocol client under a dedicated root key; URL approvals were not merged into host permission rules.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: On startup/hydration path for host configuration; setting-change propagation is off active tool execution unless it races a new request.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Persist host config by writing a temporary file and renaming it
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One write plus one rename for each persisted config update, serialized by the existing persistence chain.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: One direct write was performed; the rename adds one filesystem operation to prevent partial reads.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Persistence follows config updates; not on rendering/input hot paths.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Number of configured approval rules and frequency of user settings changes, normally small and infrequent.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: The forwarder coalesces structurally equal values; host persistence is chained/serialized, and no subprocess or network boundary is introduced.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Structural equality suppresses unchanged dispatches; root state supplies the current permission value. No cold/warm distinction beyond host hydration and filesystem cache.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Very large user rule tables increase conversion/allocation linearly, but realistic tables are small.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression; work is bounded by infrequent configuration changes and existing equality/serialization guards.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 54 changed files and relevant call paths. Reported duplicate filesystem path resolution and uncached serial Git-root probing on file approval paths; shell parsing, settings mirroring, config synchronization, persistence, IPC, cache behavior, and concurrency did not produce additional high-confidence regressions.
